Family Health

Brown urine: possible causes, tests and when to get help

Updated: November 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Brown urine can be unsettling, especially when you otherwise feel well. It may reflect a medicine or food, concentrated urine, blood, or pigments associated with a problem elsewhere in the body. The colour alone cannot tell these apart. This guide concerns adults, including women; being on a period or having no pain should not automatically end the assessment.

Start with the symptoms that change urgency

Get urgent medical advice for brown urine that might contain blood, even if it happens once, is painless or you are uncertain. Yellow eyes or skin, markedly reduced urine, swelling, fever with side or back pain, or vomiting also need prompt assessment. During pregnancy, contact your maternity or medical service promptly about unexplained brown urine or suspected urinary infection. Do not wait for every warning sign to appear.

Seek emergency help for confusion, unusual difficulty waking, collapse or serious breathing difficulty. Inability to pass urine with a painful swollen lower abdomen also needs emergency assessment. Dark urine after intense exercise or heat exposure, especially with unusual muscle pain or weakness, needs immediate medical attention. A plan to drink more and check again later must not delay these responses.

Concentration is one possibility, not a colour diagnosis

Urine often becomes darker yellow when there is less water in it. Heat, sweating, vomiting, diarrhoea or difficulty drinking can contribute. Thirst, a dry mouth, dizziness and passing less urine are useful additional clues. A tea-brown sample cannot safely be assumed to be ordinary mild dehydration, and clear-looking brown urine is not reassuring simply because it is not cloudy.

Drink normally according to your needs and any medical fluid plan while arranging advice. Small sips may be easier if you feel sick, but inability to keep fluids down or continuing low output needs help. Do not force large volumes, particularly with kidney or heart disease or a prescribed fluid restriction. Trying to achieve a particular shade is not a substitute for finding the cause.

Check recent foods and the exact medicine

Beetroot and some other strongly coloured foods can change urine appearance; rhubarb may also alter its colour. A food history helps, but the resulting shade varies and cannot prove that food explains a new brown sample. Note what you ate, when the colour began and whether it returns. Unexplained, persistent or recurrent discoloration deserves a check rather than repeated reassurance from a food list.

Some antibiotics, laxatives and other medicines can change urine colour. For example, nitrofurantoin can make it yellow-brown without this alone meaning harm. However, jaundice, pale stools, severe illness or other new symptoms may indicate a different problem or a serious medicine reaction. Ask a pharmacist or prescriber about the exact product and what to do; do not simply wait to finish a course or stop necessary treatment to test a theory. Follow urgent advice and the product’s instructions if a serious reaction is suspected.

Blood and menstrual contamination require different checks

Blood in urine, called hematuria, can look pink, red or brown. Possible explanations include infection, stones, injury, kidney inflammation and, less commonly, cancer. The amount of pain and the shade cannot reliably rank these causes. A clinician may need urine testing and further assessment even after the colour disappears.

Menstrual or other vaginal blood can mix with a urine sample. Tell the clinician whether you are bleeding so they can advise collection and, when appropriate, repeat the test after the period. This does not mean that all brown urine during menstruation can be ignored. Burning, urgency, fever or flank pain needs its own assessment; see https://bemamas.com/family-health/painful-urination-causes-and-when-to-seek-care/

Kidney inflammation can follow an earlier infection

Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is an immune reaction affecting the kidney’s filtering units after certain throat or skin infections. It is different from bacteria directly causing a kidney infection. It may develop days to weeks after the earlier illness, including when that illness seems to have improved. Children are affected more often, but adults can develop it too.

Reddish-brown urine, swelling around the eyes or limbs, reduced urine and high blood pressure may occur. This pattern needs prompt assessment with blood pressure measurement and urine and blood tests. Appearance cannot identify this particular kidney disease. Treatment addresses the findings and any remaining infection; leftover antibiotics are not a safe response to dark urine.

Liver and bile problems can add a different pigment

Bilirubin is made as red blood cells are recycled and is normally processed by the liver. Some liver or bile-drainage problems allow a water-soluble form to enter urine. Dark urine alongside yellow eyes or skin, pale stools or itching therefore needs urgent medical advice. Hepatitis A, B and C are among possible liver infections, but hepatitis also has nonviral causes and may cause few symptoms. Fever, fatigue, nausea or poor appetite are clues to discuss, not a way to identify the virus.

Cirrhosis is long-term liver damage and can be silent early on. Later changes may include jaundice, abdominal or leg swelling and confusion. Urine colour neither diagnoses cirrhosis nor tells you its severity. Someone with known cirrhosis who develops vomiting of blood, black stools or sudden confusion needs emergency care. For an explanation of laboratory results rather than a colour-based diagnosis, see https://bemamas.com/family-health/bilirubin-blood-test-jaundice-results/

After strenuous activity, think beyond dehydration

Damaged muscle can release substances into the blood, including myoglobin, which may darken urine. Severe muscle breakdown is called rhabdomyolysis. Unexpectedly strong muscle pain, weakness or tea-coloured urine after strenuous exertion, heat or injury needs immediate assessment. Symptoms may appear hours or days later, and you do not need to have all of them before seeking help.

Stop the activity and obtain medical attention rather than trying another workout or waiting for the urine to clear. Clinicians use blood creatine kinase, often repeated, together with the overall assessment. A home urine strip or a sample without obvious blood cannot safely exclude rhabdomyolysis. Treatment may need hospital monitoring; drinking water alone is not a reliable treatment plan.

Red-cell breakdown differs from ordinary iron deficiency

Hemolytic anemia occurs when red blood cells are destroyed faster than the body can replace them. It can arise from inherited blood conditions, immune reactions, infections or some medicines. In certain forms, released blood pigment contributes to dark urine. Tiredness, dizziness, weakness or jaundice may accompany it, but none of these symptoms alone establishes hemolysis.

A blood count and further tests help determine whether red cells are breaking down and why. Not every type of anemia causes brown urine, and taking iron is not a general treatment for this finding. Tell the team about known blood disorders, new medicines and a recent transfusion. Sudden severe illness, fainting or breathing difficulty needs emergency care instead of waiting for a routine anemia appointment.

Unusual causes need the right context

Babesiosis is caused by a parasite that infects red blood cells, often after a tick bite. It can cause fever, chills, body aches and fatigue; red-cell destruction may produce jaundice and dark urine. Mention recent travel, outdoor exposure, a tick bite or a blood transfusion when relevant. Diagnosis requires appropriate blood testing, and some people become seriously ill. Brown urine on its own does not make this the likely explanation.

Exceptionally, case reports describe darkening or black urine associated with pigment production in advanced melanoma. This is a rare observation, not a routine cause of brown urine or a home cancer test. A new or changing skin lesion deserves its own assessment, while the urine change should be investigated on its actual clinical findings. Searching for rare diagnoses should not postpone the more immediate checks.

Let the history guide urine and blood testing

Tell the clinician when the colour first appeared, whether it happens every time, how much urine you pass, and whether there is pain, fever, jaundice, swelling or muscle weakness. Bring your medicines and supplements list and mention exercise, injury, foods, menstrual bleeding, recent infections and pregnancy. Follow the collection instructions for a fresh urine sample; do not deliberately overdrink to make it look normal.

Testing may include urinalysis and microscopy, a urine culture when infection is suspected, kidney and liver blood tests, and a blood count. Muscle symptoms may prompt creatine kinase testing; suspected red-cell breakdown needs different blood tests. Imaging or a specialist examination is selected when the findings justify it. Not everyone needs every investigation, and a single urine-strip result does not identify every pigment or cause.

Agree on results and reassessment

Ask who will contact you with results, when that should happen and what to do if the colour returns. Treatment may involve an infection plan, a medicine review or care for a kidney, liver, blood or muscle condition. It is directed at the cause rather than the shade. Antibiotics, iron, herbal cleanses or extra water are not interchangeable remedies.

A reassuring first test does not settle persistent or recurrent unexplained symptoms. Contact the service again and report new pain, fever, yellowing, swelling, reduced output or weakness. A previous diagnosis should be part of the assessment, rather than an automatic explanation for a new episode. Keep the individual follow-up plan, and use urgent or emergency care when the warning symptoms described above develop.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Arrange advice based on suspected blood and associated symptoms rather than judging the exact shade.

Use food, medicine, exercise and bleeding history to guide targeted urine and blood tests.

Agree a result and follow-up plan, and seek earlier care if symptoms change.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you note colour changes, symptom timing, medicines and questions for an appointment. It cannot distinguish blood from other pigments, diagnose kidney or liver disease, or decide whether a medicine should be stopped. Do not delay care to complete a record.

When to seek help

Possible blood in urine, new jaundice or markedly reduced output needs urgent advice. Dark urine after exertion with unusual muscle pain or weakness needs immediate medical attention. Confusion, difficulty waking, collapse, serious breathing difficulty or inability to pass urine with a painful swollen abdomen needs emergency care. Do not treat an unexplained change with forced fluids or unprescribed medicines.

Evidence notes updated: November 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Brown urine can involve concentration, food, medicine, blood or another pigment.
  • Possible urine blood needs urgent advice even once or without pain.
  • Jaundice, reduced urine, swelling or systemic illness changes the urgency.
  • Dark urine after exertion with muscle symptoms needs immediate assessment.
  • Tests and follow-up should identify the cause; colour alone cannot do that.

Frequently asked questions

Can diet change the colour of urine?

Yes. Foods such as beetroot and rhubarb can alter the appearance, but the shade varies. Tell the clinician what you ate; do not assume that food explains persistent, recurrent or unexplained brown urine, especially if you feel unwell or suspect blood.

Can medicines make urine brown?

Some can. Nitrofurantoin is one example of an expected yellow-brown change. The exact product and accompanying symptoms matter: jaundice, pale stools or serious illness need prompt advice. Ask the pharmacist or prescriber what to do instead of stopping treatment yourself or waiting for the course to finish.

Does anemia cause dark urine?

Certain forms involving rapid red-cell destruction can do so. This is different from saying that every anemia, including iron deficiency, makes urine brown. Blood tests help identify the cause; do not start iron solely because of urine colour.

What should an athlete do about brown urine?

Stop strenuous activity and get immediate medical attention, particularly with unexpected muscle pain or weakness. Muscle breakdown can look like dehydration and may appear later after exertion. Do not rely on water, a home urine strip or a promised waiting period to rule it out.

Can I ignore brown urine during my period?

No. Menstrual blood can contaminate a sample, but it does not explain every episode. Tell the clinician so collection or repeat testing can be planned. Possible urine blood, pain, fever or ongoing discoloration still needs assessment.

Does brown urine mean liver disease?

Not necessarily. Liver or bile problems are one possibility, especially with yellow eyes or skin, pale stools or itching. Blood, muscle pigment and other explanations also exist. New jaundice needs urgent advice, while tests establish which pathway applies.

Will drinking a large amount of water clear the problem?

It may dilute the colour without treating its cause. Drink appropriately for your medical circumstances, but do not force water or delay care for suspected blood, severe muscle symptoms, jaundice or reduced output. Follow any prescribed fluid restriction.

What if it disappears before my appointment?

Still report suspected blood and keep the advised assessment. Note the timing and any accompanying symptoms or medicine changes. Follow-up is particularly important if the colour returns; a temporary improvement does not establish why it happened.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
